Fishing Industry-Beam Trawlers

subtopic: FISHING INDUSTRY-LICENSING OF BEAM TRAWLERS IN NOVA SCOTIA WATERS

speechtext: Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: FISHING INDUSTRY-LICENSING OF BEAM TRAWLERS IN NOVA SCOTIA WATERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to take advantage of this motion to bring to the attention of the house a matter that is of great importance to the fishing industry, especially in the province of Nova Scotia. I refer to the annual licensing of beam trawlers, sometimes called steam trawlers, I suppose because they are propelled by steam. The immediate reason for bringing forward this matter at the present time is that before April 1 the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud) must make up his mind whether he will renew the licences already existing; whether he will receive new applications or, on the other hand, whether he will cancel the licences that exist at the present time. My purpose at the moment is to make an appeal to him, in addition to the representations I have already made, in the interests of the hook and line fishermen of the Atlantic mast.
This matter is controlled by an order in council dated August 29, 1931, which provides:
1. A licence for a fishing vessel using an otter or other trawl of a similar nature, other than a small dragger operated by inshore fishermen, will not be' granted, except under the following conditions:
(a) That the applicant for such licence shall furnish the Minister of Fisheries with evidence that will satisfy the said minister that he cannot obtain an adequate supply of suitable fish to enable him properly to conduct and develop his business from the hook and line fishermen, and that if the licence is granted, the extent of his purchase of fresh fish from the said fishermen will not be adversely affected.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that there are two conditions necessary for the granting of a licence; first that the operator cannot obtain a suitable supply of fish from the hook and line fishermen, and second that his purchases from these fishermen will not be adversely affected if he obtains a licence. He must satisfy the Minister of Fisheries, according to the provisions of this order in council.
I do not like this order in council. Each year this matter comes up and the Minister of Fisheries must make a decision. The hook and line fishermen who desire to promote their industry and who wish to build vessels are not able to do so because of the insecurity brought about by this legislation, since they never know what is going to happen each year

when this question comes up for consideration. Then again, it puts the Minister of Fisheries on the spot each year, and it seems to me hardly fair that he should be made the umpire, as it were, between different forms of fishing.
I claim that the situation is such that licences should be refused for the year 1939. In the first place there is no question that the corporations can get an adequate supply of fish from the hook and line fishermen; in fact there is an over supply of fish on the Atlantic coast, as there has been for some years. Only the other day we were told by men interested in the business that the cold storages along the coast were full of fish, and that the great difficulty was to get a market for them. There are several large companies on the Atlantic coast engaged in the distribution of fish, but only one company has the privilege of trawling. If trawling is a good thing and something that should be promoted in the fishing industry, why should just this, one company have that privilege? Again, in the interests of employment I think the decision this year should go to the hook and line fishermen. In January, 1938, the one company using trawlers employed nine Lunenburg vessels and 225 men. Then when the fishing season started in the fall of 1938 they laid off five vessels and employed only four of the hook and line vessels. This meant that 125 men in my constituency became unemployed, and for every man unemployed in the primary enterprise there are about three others also unemployed in the allied industries.
I wonder if there was ever any definite matter considered by this house that was looked into by so many commissions, and in connection with which the reports of these commissions were not accepted to the extent that is the case here. In the first place we had the Maclean commission, which went throughout Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and down to the Magdalen islands. The majority report of that commission contained this recommendation:
With mounting density of population and a much larger consumption of fish, it is possible that in some future time steam trawlers may be required in Canada to meet the demands of a large fish consuming population. But that time seems to us to be very far distant. And meanwhile, steam trawlers should in our judgment, without fear of the consequence, be prohibited from landing their fish and from obtaining supplies at Canadian ports, in order that the fishing population of the maritime provinces may be protected and retained.

Fishing Industry-Beam Trawlers
It is only fair to say that the minority report of the chairman, who is now Judge Maclean, dissented from the majority report. He submitted a report of his own, in which he said:
The number of trawlers in use should not exceed that number which will produce from time to time the market requirements in excess of boat and vessel production. The interest of trawler owners and general public interests would be best served by such a policy, and no sacrifice would be required in its adoption.
Of all the commissioners, Mr. Speaker, who have investigated this matter of trawling on the Atlantic coast the opinion of Judge Maclean is the only one except that of Mr. Young of the price spreads, which did not definitely say that the use of the beam trawler should be prohibited.
This matter has been receiving consideration in Nova Scotia during the past week. A resolution was introduced into the local legislature which reads as follows:
Whereas a majority of the royal commission, provincial economic inquiry, 1934, appointed under an act of this legislature, found that the beam trawler "should not be permitted to operate" and recommended "that its use be prohibited";
Therefore resolve that this house urges upon the dominion government and parliament the need for early action to terminate beam trawler operations as recommended by said committee.
This resolution was debated for two days in the provincial legislature, and only two members of the legislature who spoke registered their opinions in favour of the trawlers. A member of the government who on the main motion had spoken against the trawler moved the following amendment:
That this government requests the Minister of Fisheries to grant no licences to beam or otter trawlers for the year 1939 until it is definitely known and decided that Nova Scotian hook and line fishermen cannot furnish an adequate supply of suitable fish.
Thus it was indicated to the federal authorities that before they permit the operation of the beam trawlers it should be definitely known that the hook and line fishermen cannot supply the needs of the fishing industry. In this regard the Minister of Fisheries has the complete say as to what shall be done. There is no appeal from his decision. As I said before, every year this burden is put upon him.
Then there was a commission in Nova Scotia called the Jones commission. On the Jones commission sat a professor of the University of Toronto; also Mr. Alex. Johnston, at one time federal deputy minister of Fisheries. That commission asked for the abolition of the trawler.
I come now to what has been known as the price spreads committee, followed by a royal commission appointed by the government, which went exhaustively into the matter of beam trawlers. The commission reported as follows:-
This argument that the trawlers are necessary to provide continuity of supply, has been advanced on previous occasions, and before other commissions investigating the fishing industry. It has, indeed, been the heart of the case in favour of the trawler. We feel, however, that the new type of fishing vessel known as the Lunenburg auxiliary schooner, the development of which has recently been so successful, offers all the advantages of continuity of supply possessed by the trawler and at the same time utilizes more fishing labour, a point which we consider of great importance. We feel, therefore, that under present conditions, trawler operations should be gradually discontinued by government prohibition.
Can we lightly cast aside the findings of three such important commissions? Was there ever a matter so exhaustively investigated, and upon which there seems to have been so much unanimity of opinion on the part of those who have visited the field? In the department, at Ottawa, where men do their work at desks and by correspondence, we find that there is a difference of opinion. But any man who is sent down into the field to see conditions as they really are comes back with the view that the trawler is not necessary and that our social and economic problems would be better served by sticking to the hook and line fishermen.
The fact that there are three trawlers in Nova Scotia does not tell the whole story. The trawler makes of the fish corporation a primary producer; he uses that instrument as a club which he holds over the heads of the fishermen of the country in order that he may control prices. The fishermen have no bargaining power, because the company with the three trawlers say to the fisherman, when he comes in, "I have a trawler coming in tomorrow; if you do not take the price I will give you, I do not need your fish."
The buying of fish in Nova Scotia is highly centralized. Three big companies do the buying, namely the National Fish Company, Lunenburg Sea Products, and General Seafoods, and it is my opinion that they work pretty closely together. I think also that they control to a large extent the prices paid to fishermen. The Lunenburg Sea Products organization is the most successful fishing corporation on the Atlantic coast. They buy fish from all parts of Nova Scotia. They have fleets of vessels under their own management, and working in cooperation with the fishermen. They do not use trawlers. It is the most

Fishing Industry-Beam Trawlers
successful company on the coast, and it seems to me that that is evidence that a company can get a suitable supply of fish without having trawlers.
It might be said that we have a new market in the United States, and that therefore trawlers are necessary. I must advise the house that the United States fishermen were somewhat concerned about the trade agreement, because they said we were going to flood their market. The report came out that they were going to restrict the action of their trawlers from the port of Boston. But one of the principal items in the treaty is fillets, which go in under a quota of 15,000,000 pounds, being 9,000,000 pounds extra per year, amounting to about 27,000,000 pounds of round fish. The three trawlers now operating from Nova Scotia can produce just about that 27,000,000 pounds of fish, which will 'be necessary to make the fillets to fill the quota for the United States market.
We have an over-supply, and we are told that we should have trawlers because the United States fishermen have trawlers. We are told about two hundred trawlers and all this sort of thing. The United States fishermen have seventy trawlers. I have a telegram before me from Mr. E. H. Cooley, president of the American Fishermen's Association, who tells me that they have seventy trawlers. But the United States people import fish, they cannot get a supply sufficient for their demand, and we regard the United States market as a splendid market for Canadian fish. When it is argued that because the United States fishermen have seventy trawlers we should have seventy, I say simply this, that we dd not need trawlers at the present time, and that the fishermen of the maritime provinces want to make a living.

subtopic: FISHING INDUSTRY-LICENSING OF BEAM TRAWLERS IN NOVA SCOTIA WATERS
speechtext: If they do not need them in the fishing industry, why do they buy them? If they have seventy trawlers in the United States, perhaps they should also have trawlers in Canada.

subtopic: FISHING INDUSTRY-LICENSING OF BEAM TRAWLERS IN NOVA SCOTIA WATERS
speechtext:
I do not think that is any argument that we should have them in Canada. The question is whether you do or do not need them. They were able to get them from Great Britain at a low price.
Some beam trawler advocates argue that they can produce fish cheaper than the hook and line fishermen. I refer hon. members to what was brought out in the evidence given before the price spreads commission and what is stated in the Maclean report. It was stated there that the cost of producing fish by beam trawler is $1.89 per hundred pounds. That was the cost some years ago, and it is likely higher 
to-day. At no time do the fishermen receive more than a cent and a half per pound on the average for their fish from the trawler companies. These companies are able to save money by buying fish from the fishermen, and they get better fish. According to the evidence given before the price spreads commission by a former president of one of the fish companies, these companies preferred trawlers because it gave them better control of the industry and of prices; they were an instrument by which they were able to control their business without regard to the human element. They were able to get along without bargaining with the fishermen when they wanted to buy fish.
The hook and line method is not inadequate, nor is it uneconomical. The Lunenburg fishing schooner is the most economical fishing machine in the world. The companies owning trawlers recognize this fact. Two new vessels have been built after the fashion of the Lunenburg fishing schooner, and they are now being operated successfully out of Halifax. The fisherman is much better off with the hook and line method of fishing. The cost of a fishing schooner is within the range of the pocket-books of a group of fishermen, whereas a beam trawler is such an expensive machine that only a corporation can purchase it. Anyone in Nova Scotia who wants to engage in hook and line fishing can easily secure a schooner. In Lunenburg this method of fishing is a cooperative enterprise, every vessel usually being divided into 64 shares. Any young man who thinks he is fit to command a vessel can go around among the people of the town and county and sell shares in it. Sometimes those who work on the vessel have shares. This has proved to be the most successful method of fishing in Nova Scotia.
It seems to me we would go far towards solving the great problem of unemployment if the production of fish in Nova Scotia were left in the hands of the hook and line fishermen. What is the argument advanced by the trawler companies? They contend that the Americans use trawlers. I say the United States must import fish because they are unable to supply their own market. On the other hand, there are many fishermen along the Atlantic coast who cannot find employment. In former years the Nova Scotia fisherman could go to New England and ship out on a vessel from Gloucester or Boston, but the immigration laws of the United States do not permit that to-day. These men are in Nova Scotia and our main idea should be to find employment for them.
The trawler companies contend that there are certain kinds of fish which cannot be caught

Fishing Industry-Beam Trawlers
by the hook and line fishermen. For several years they came here with the argument that they wanted to catch rose fish. This fish is caught in deep water; it is a soft-fleshed fish caught principally along the coast of the United States. Its selling price is quite low and there is no profit in it for anyone except these large corporations who want to dump it on certain markets. Recently it was found that this fish had a parasite and I understand the health authorities of the United States have had trouble about its use in many of the western states. Fish from Canada enter the United States under a quota, and if we allow this quota to be filled by redfish caught by the beam trawlers, they will replace the higher priced fish which should ibe going into the United States market.
The trawler companies contend also that they want continuity of supply. The Lunenburg fishing schooner is a more mobile unit than the beam trawler, and it is cheaper to operate. These schooners are equipped with radio telephones and are propelled by diesel engines. They can be brought in and out of port more quickly and are much less expensive to operate. Last year we were told by the trawler companies that they wanted fast transportation. A beam trawler will average nine knots an hour, but a fishing schooner can go from nine to twelve knots an hour. Fish caught one day on the banks can be on the market the next day. When it comes to transportation, the diesel schooner is far ahead of the beam trawler, and their record of continuity is splendid.
Most of these old arguments have been dropped. We are now told that they want these trawlers so that they may catch a few flounders which are probably sold on the English market. The line fisherman can also catch flounders, but when the fishermen bring in too many, the companies use their judgment as to whether they shall buy them. There is one thing which must be admitted about the beam trawler, it is a safer way to fish. However, there is a suggestion now being put forth in connection with the schooners that in addition to the use of dories, they use a long rubber covered line which can be hauled in over the bow and which goes in over the stern. This method will practically double their capacity, and will make the operation of these schooners even more economical. The long line and dory method of fishing from the schooner will make fishing practically as safe as with the beam trawler.
Then we are told that while all this will help the Lunenburg fishermen, it will not help the shore fisherman. If we have an over supply of fish on our markets, if these companies can get their supplies of fish without going to the fishermen, the shore fishermen will suffer. Do you not think that the shore fishermen would be benefited if these companies were obliged to send out their buyers to buy fish from them? There would then be a seller's market instead of a buyer's market in the fishing industry in Nova Scotia.
Hook and line fishermen buy large quantities of bait from the shore fishermen. The hook and line fishermen have built up towns and communities in the province of Nova Scotia. They have helped to establish the allied industries-the sail maker, the blacksmith, the block maker and the shipbuilder; but in view of the insecurity that exists today in the fishing industry people will not build vessels in Nova Scotia now.
The shore fisherman lives on the headlands along the shore, and he must be there to catch the mackerel, the herring, the lobster, and the seasonal fish that frequent those waters at certain seasons of the year. We all know that the headland is the proper place for the shore fisherman to live. But if you take away his backlog, which is the cod fishery, a vital element in making up his revenue, it will make conditions such that the shore fisherman cannot make a living. The first consideration, Mr. Speaker, should be given to the fisherman who lives in the outport and who must maintain himself there for the purpose of carrying on certain of the fisheries of this country, and the cod fishery should be preserved for him.
Suppose someone says that we should allow the beam trawlers to operate; and suppose they increase until you have eight or ten or twelve beam trawlers. There will then be no room for anybody else in the fishing industry in Nova Scotia, and what will you do? You will make of them slum dwellers in the city.
Our shore fishermen are skilled workers. They live in humble homes, it is true, but in healthy homes along the shore of the province where they can bring up their families in wholesome surroundings and get an education in the rural districts; and the rural people are after all the backbone of this country. Anything that tends to centralize this industry in one big port is bad for the province of Nova Scotia. There is no reason why the hook and line fishermen should not be sustained. The menace of the trawler should not be allowed to grow; I contend that for the year 1939 no licences should be issued to the beam trawlers.
There has been a lot of propaganda in this country in favour of the trawler. Some

Fishing Industry-Beam Trawlers
months ago I observed in the Financial Post an article headed, "Truce in the trawler war." The article goes on to say:
A skilful manoeuvre directed, it is believed, by dominion government officials, has transformed the opposing armies in the maritime trawler battle into comrades in arms-though not perhaps yet in each other's arms.
In a letter to the editor of the Financial Post I said that I did not think this article correctly portrayed the situation as regards either the fishermen or the general public, and I asked to be permitted to write an article for the Financial Post. They sent one of their representatives here and I had a discussion with him. I saw him upstairs, and I expected that the Financial Post would invite me to write the article. Their representative said that the article that had appeared in the Financial Post had been prepared by their own correspondent in the interests of the public. But the Financial Post did not permit me to write an article to be reproduced in that paper in the interests of the public, and I have not yet been granted that privilege.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, under the order in council you are not permitted to have a trawler unless you cannot get an adequate supply of fish from the hook and line fishermen. I claim also that the purchases from the hook and line fishermen should not be adversely affected, as undoubtedly they have been. The burden was put upon the minister to decide, and he must decide before next Saturday.
I liked better the order in council of 1929. Hon. members will recall that when the Hon. Mr. Cardin was minister of fisheries he visited the maritime provinces, and after he came back to Ottawa legislation was passed by parliament amending the Fisheries Act. Under section 56 beam trawling was not permitted except under certain conditions. This led to an order in council which practically prohibited beam trawling, because the order in council of 1929 stipulated that the trawler must be built in Canada and provided for the payment of a tax which would have been prohibitive and would have driven the trawlers out of business. The trawler companies refused to pay the tax and took the matter to the courts. After the case had been before the courts for some time it was withdrawn, and the money thaw had been paid in taxes by some companies was refunded.
The order in council under which we are working to-day is the one under which the minister must act in dealing with this problem.
Parliament has spoken on this question; three commissions have also spoken. An order in council was passed in 1929, which is said

to be ultra vires, but which expressed the opinion of the government and parliament of this country. All the evidence is against the trawler, yet the companies concerned are able to convince people in this part of the country that beam trawlers are necessary in the fishing industry. But the people that we should sustain in the province of Nova Scotia are the hook and line fishermen. We are told that we are against progress. We come here and say to you that what parliament has done in the past should be invoked now, that the time is even more opportune for prohibiting beam trawlers.
While I know this is a difficult question, and while I appreciate the difficulties of the Minister of Fisheries in view of the contending interests who prosecute the fisheries in this country, the evidence is wholly on the side of the hook and line fishemen. I trust that when the minister makes his decision he will see to it that the interests of these fishermen are preserved and protected so that once the industry is stabilized it can go forward- and be a benefit to the whole province of Nova Scotia.
Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre) Mr. Speaker, while I have no expert knowledge of the fishing industry, representations have been made to me as to the position in which the fishermen are placed, and as representing one of the groups in this house I feel I could not let the opportunity pass without endorsing what has just been said by the hon. member for Queens-Lunen-burg (Mr. Kinley). I have no desire to go over the ground which he has so fully covered. As I have looked into the situation, one or two points appeal to me which I should like to bring before the house.
First.of all, these licences for trawling are being given as a special privilege. The applicant for the licence must convince the Minister of Fisheries that he cannot obtain from the hook and line fishermen an adequate supply of suitable fish to enable him properly to conduct and develop his business. The hook and line fishermen claim very emphatically that that condition does not prevail, that they are able to provide an adequate supply of fish. Futhermore, they claim that even under the new arrangements that have been made under the treaty they can fill the entire quota without any assistance from the trawlers. It is quite obvious that members of parliament cannot go into that technical matter, although sometimes it seems to us from the west that members from eastern Canada discuss the question of growing wheat, and matters of that kind. However, these are matters for the specialist.

.	Fishing Industry-Beam Trawlers
I would emphasize what the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg has said, that every royal commission appointed by the government in the past ten years, including the price spreads committee, consisting of members of parliament, has recommended the abolition of the trawler. With that situation prevailing, it seems to me the minister should be able to produce overwhelming evidence to show why the granting of licences should be continued.
A few weeks ago, on March 11, there was published in the Halifax Herald an interesting table showing what the fishermen get and what the consumer has to pay. I am quoting from the table. Fresh cod per pound is li cents to the fisherman and 15 cents to the consumer. That is the information this newspaper gives, and I am quoting as I stated from a table published in the Halifax Herald of March 11. Perhaps it is only fair to say that there are some losses, as noted here, in cutting off the heads, fins, tails and so on. Still that is a tremendous spread, and it may indicate some of the reasons why the ordinary fisherman feels that he ought to have a fair break in this matter. Not only, he thinks, is it a matter of his being able to fill the quota, but in addition to that, this arrangement by which the trawlers are not only fishermen but also dealers gives an unfair advantage to the trawlers, and this seems to be the result.
I should not like to be considered as one who is in any way blocking the natural progress in the development of the best means of getting fish. I know something about the difficulties with which we are faced in regard to trawlers on the Pacific coast. I do not know whether the same difficulties obtain on the Atlantic. But under these circumstances, 71492-147
with the information before the house, it seems to me that the minister should consider very carefully the whole situation before giving licences to the trawlers.

subtopic: FISHING INDUSTRY-LICENSING OF BEAM TRAWLERS IN NOVA SCOTIA WATERS
speechtext:
I wish to correct an impression that has 'been left by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) with regard to the price of fillets. A fillet is about a third of the fish, and I should be very much surprised if fillets sold at less than from five to six cents per pound. That would be a fairer price. That is as I understand the situation, and I make that remark in order to give a fairer picture of it. Two cents a pound is altogether too low for fresh fillets, unless there is a glut or something of the kind.
I have heard a great deal about the beam trawler, and I think I can truly say that I have given more thought and consideration to this one item than to any other single question connected with the fishing industry. As far back as I can remember, the fishermen in my constituency have been almost unanimous in their opposition to the trawler.

subtopic: FISHING INDUSTRY-LICENSING OF BEAM TRAWLERS IN NOVA SCOTIA WATERS
speechtext: What about the local member?

subtopic: FISHING INDUSTRY-LICENSING OF BEAM TRAWLERS IN NOVA SCOTIA WATERS
speechtext:
I am speaking of the fishermen in my constituency. I have no doubt the hon. gentleman is referring to the member for Digby county. The district of Clare, which forms a part of my constituency, is opposed to the beam trawler. That takes care of the remark of my hon. friend. The feeling has been that the 'beam trawler and the hook and line fisherman cannot exist side by side when both are given an unrestricted field. That is to say, the market for our fish is not such that you could allow a number of beam trawlers to operate without any restriction whatever, because in the end they would take over the production from the hook and line fishermen. That is the view of the fishermen in my district, and it dates back to a time during the war and afterward.
In 1910 we had one beam trawler; in 1913 five; in 1915, four; in 1917, six; in 1918, eight; in 1919, seven; in 1921, six; in 1923, seven; in 1925, nine; in 1927, ten. At the present time we have three. The three beam trawlers now operating catch approximately one-tenth of the fish caught in Nova Scotia. I think it is fair to say that we catch about 200,000,000 pounds of ground-fish in that province, and the three beam trawlers catch about 20,000,000 pounds.
To give a fair picture of the benefits which would accrue from the abolition of the three beam trawlers, one must say that the resulting good is exaggerated. For example, in



Fishing Industry-Beam Trawlers
one of the counties I represent, the county of Yarmouth, if you abolished beam trawlers to-day and related the proportion of fish they catch to the total quantity of fish caught in Nova Scotia, you would find roughly that each fisherman had benefited to the extent of between seven and ten dollars.

Yes, per year. I think I can say that, because there is no use in exaggerating the situation. In respect to some counties that would not be true, because they catch the larger proportion of the fish, and without the 20,000,000 pounds caught by the beam trawlers it is fair to expect that they would benefit in proportion; twenty million pounds averaged at li cents a pound comes to about $300,000, and we have between 12,000 and 13,000 bounty fishermen who would be involved in the division of that sum. Some individuals of course who catch more fish would get a larger proportion of the $300,000, such as $20 or $30.
Thinking back over the years, and seeing the trend that has developed, fundamentally the issue as I see it is not only the three beam trawlers, but who is going to survive in Nova Scotia with beam trawling or hook and line fishing. Trawlers and hook and line fishing cannot exist together; with unrestricted trawling in Nova Scotia the hook and line fishermen are doomed. This is demonstrated by what has been happening for the last ten or fifteen years in Massachusetts. For some years I have gone to the fish pier every time I visited Boston, and it is easy to see what is happening there. They have unrestricted beam trawling; the number of trawlers is increasing, and the hook and line fishermen are being gradually pushed out. There are several reasons for this, but the principal one is that a man on a beam trawler in Massachusetts makes about twice the amount that the hook and line fisherman does on a fishing schooner. We have to be careful to see that we do not have in Nova Scotia a repetition of what is happening in the United States.
I speak of beam trawlers unrestricted in number. Fundamentally that is what has brought about this agitation. After the war. when the demand for fish was good, we increased the number of beam trawlers; then the demand fell off; the United States placed a tariff on fish; the West Indian and other foreign markets were affected, and the fight was on.
I do not know what view the minister has. He has to deal with the matter on the evidence submitted to him. But it should not be left in that position; we should have one

thing or the other, and the minister should not be harassed and criticized by one side and the other every year. Parliament should relieve the minister of the burden and decide whether we are to have beam trawlers or not. Then the fishermen as well as the companies would know where they stand, and it would be better for the industry generally. I suggest to the minister that if he is going to renew these licences, they should be renewed only for at the most sixty or ninety days, and in the meantime the whole question should be referred to the fisheries committee with instructions to submit definite recommendations so-that this matter may be settled once for all.
When this question goes before the committee, two or three other important matters should be considered. There is the question whether foreign trawlers should be allowed to come to our three mile limit when our own trawlers have to keep outside the twelve mile limit. At the present time hundreds of foreign beam trawlers operate on the Atlantic coast and some of them come up to the three-mile limit.

Coming now to the question before us, it seem to me a comparatively simple matter. The policy of this country-and the only policy as far as administration is concerned- that has been followed by different governments is set forth in the order in council which was read by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg. A mere order in council is a pretty weak basis for administration. Perhaps it was all right at the time, for the moment, but it would have been much better if we had crystallized that order in council into an amendment to the act which would have declared our position beyond peradven-ture. Then, as my hon. friend said a moment ago, the minister would not be badgered every year with the responsibility of coming ito a decision. However, that is the basis of [DOT]our policy. In effect that order in council .-simply says that if it can be shown that there is an insufficient supply of fresh fish from normal sources, namely the shore fishermen or the hook and line fishermen, the minister is at liberty, as a matter of emergency, shall I say, to issue trawler licences. The question arises, is there an insufficient supply of fish? Need I do more than ask the question? One of the problems with which we are confronted is the finding of markets for our fish. The senior member for Halifax (Mr. Finn) a few weeks ago discussed the question of lobsters, and in the course of that discussion the question of a market for fish came up. Last session, and again this session, the hon. member who has just taken his seat, together with other hon. members from the maritimes, made eloquent speeches pleading with parliament to do something to find extended markets for the fish of the maritimes. We are justified, I think, in concluding that there is an ample supply of fish; therefore on that ground there is no need for the issuing of trawler licences.

I propose to refer briefly to the investigation made by the price spreads committee and commission so far as it related to this matter. The subject was gone into fully, and I believe the report discloses what is really at the root of this whole problem; I shall refer to that later, after I have read a few extracts from the report. At page 175 of the report I find this paragraph:
It appears that formerly there were a number of small companies or dealers purchasing fish from the producers in practically every fishing centre along the Atlantic coast. Gradually, consolidations and amalgamations took place; some of the dealers were forced out of business; larger companies arose. For a time these larger units maintained plants along the sea coast, but later the plants located at remoter points were closed and there became apparent a general trend towards centralization. Even in communities where dealers and companies continued to operate, this trend toward centralization had its effect through a decrease in the number of those offering to purchase fish. In other words there was a local "centralization" even in instances where this did not extend to provincial " centralization."
Here I think we have largely the crux of the whole problem. There has been a gradual concentration in the processing and distribution side of the fisheries industry. I remember a year or two ago visiting some of the centres along the straits of Canso, where magnificent plants had been bought up by the large central company, and closed down; the purchase of fish in that whole district had been more or less abandoned. The result was that the fish had to be taken all the way to Halifax to find a market. Obviously this was done, of course, as a part of the business efficiency methods of the distributing and processing company, but with disregard for the convenience and indeed the welfare of the fishermen themselves.
Let me read further:
The evidence submitted to us, however, clearly indicates that there are few, if any, problems in connection with actual production.
This supports what I said a moment ago about supply.
The catch of fish in eastern Canada is ample, and, in some seasons, more than ample to meet the demands of Canadian and export markets.
That I submit in respect to the question of supply. As to earnings of fishermen, everyone knows that in the maritimes they are scandalously low. The figures given here, which prevailed in 1933-there may have been some variations since-were these :
Evidence submitted by competent witnesses indicates that the earnings of the average fisherman in the different localities of eastern Canada for the year 1933 ran from $75 to $400, according to the district in which the fisherman worked.

Of course I am not including in these figures the workmen on the trawlers. In justice I should say that these figures apply chiefly to shore fishermen. The point I wish to emphasize is that the earnings of fishermen are extremely low. The fisherman's condition is certainly very serious. That I offer further on the question of supply. The report goes on:
These low earnings are in the vast majority of cases, not due to any lack of industrious application to his work on the part of the fisherman, who works longer hours and endures more hardships than do those in many other occupations. They are the result of unfavourable economic conditions which have reflected themselves in the industry and which for the fisherman are intensified by the fact that on the side of the corporation buyer there is strong bargaining power; on his side complete or almost complete absence of such power.
Here again we have the effect of the concentration of control. Let me pause there to say this: After a close study of the problem from the standpoint of distribution and processing, and from that of the fisherman, my firm conviction is that the corporation, chiefly the largest one, desires to have the trawler so that he may have large quantities of fish which will enable him to control the market price of fish from the hook and line fishermen and from the shore fishermen. The minister shakes his head. He may differ from me, and others may differ. But that is my firm conviction, after a careful study of the whole business. I am convinced from the evidence which we heard from the heads of the corporation itself as well as from others-and there were several days of it- that the main reason for the persistent demand for the existence of the trawler is to maintain control over the supply of fish.
If we take the argument they have advanced and treat it seriously, we find it is this. They say that there is a fluctuation in the flow of supply from the hook and line and shore fishermen. That is challenged; however it is their argument. Therefore in order to maintain a steady supply to the markets of Montreal, Toronto and other points in upper Canada, they must have the trawlers. Their argument is that if they cannot have the trawlers, they may break down in their distribution to these centres. I do not consider the argument worthy of very much consideration.

No; there was very little consideration for the consumer. And I am not at all satisfied with the method of distribution of fish, despite all this [DOT] boasting of efficiency on the part of the larger corporation. There is perhaps an improvement, but I doubt if there is very much. We can show extensions of business here and there. But, for example, let us consider the city of Ottawa: Anyone interested in fish merchandizing who will walk around this city and see the way maritime fish is offered to the consumer here will wonder that as much of it is consumed. Possibly so. But what I am getting at is that we are always willing to find some almost visionary excuse for the distributor-in this instance the distributing company; but it is always at the expense of the fisherman. Here we are, going over this problem year after year, although the facts and conditions have been known for ten or fifteen years. We know about the problems of the fishermen, but outside of some little grant here or some little sop or palliative there, we are doing little or nothing to meet their needs. The first thing we ought to do is to endeavour to get the producing end of this business on a sound footing.
Let us consider the interjection made a moment ago by the Minister of National Revenue with regard to the question of

supply. Any study of the . history of the industry will disclose the fact-and the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg will set me right if I am astray-that within the last ten or twelve years the schooners from Lunenburg have developed a technique in connection with hook and line fishing which is a great credit to the fishermen of that district. I am told by those who are competent to judge that in its essence the Lunenburg schooner is equal or superior to the trawler, except that it does not sweep up huge quantities of fish in a short time. Steady progress has been made in the last ten or fifteen years by the producers of fish in improving their methods. I am told that these splendid schooners now surpass anything in the world as a fishing instrument. The supply of fish is just as soundly assured as it would be through the operation of trawlers.
There is another question to be considered, that of conservation. I know that this will be brushed aside, but it should be considered nevertheless. I am not advancing this argument with a view to doing away with the trawler because of destructive methods; I am simply saying it is a factor which should be considered, particularly where we have assured an ample continuous supply. The trawler sweeps the 'bottom of the fishing areas; it sweeps into the ship all sorts of immature fish, poor fish and good fish. I am told there is a possibility of the trawler destroying the marine vegetable life on the ocean floor, which may have some effect upon our fisheries. These are questions to be determined by the fishery experts. I believe they are divided in their opinions, but one thing is certain, that the trawler method of fishing is not helpful to the conservation of fish. At least we can dogmatize on that point.

In its report, after considering all the factors, the question of supply, the low wages TMr. Stevens.]
paid to the fishermen, the processing costs, the consumer interest, and so on, the commission made this recommendation at page 198:
This board might be known as the "Fisheries Control Board" and should be restricted only by the terms and provisions of the marketing act. The proposed board should not in the first instance attempt to institute revolutionary reforms, as affecting various branches of the industry, but should proceed through successive steps to eliminate, in logical order, the more pressing disabilities. Its most important duty would be to make every possible effort to ensure that the fishermen secure a fair price for his fish and not, as at present, the pittance that is left over from the consumer's dollar after all other branches of the industry have received their share. The board might next approach the problem arising from conditions in domestic retail markets.
Let me pause to give utterance to a bit of philosophy of mine with regard to the primary producer, not only of fish but of other products as well. The first duty of parliament, indeed I would say the first duty of all students of economics who have the welfare of Canada at heart, should be to see that the primary producer receives a fair return for his effort. That should be the fundamental principle underlying all our economic thinking. It is the basis of whatever I may have in the way of philosophy in approaching economic problems. The same applies to the farmer. I am sorry to say that many approach this question from the point of view of what they call the consumer's dollar-page the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman). They take what they call the consumer's dollar, and out of that must come distribution costs, transportation, processing costs and the profits of these various activities. The primary producer gets what is left. My argument is that it should be exactly the reverse. There should be a fair return to the primaiy producer, in this instance the fisherman, and upon that you should erect your costs. Then it should be the duty of parliament or other public bodies to scrutinize carefully the subsequent charges and costs, such as processing, distribution and so on, to see that there is no unfair exploitation of the consumer. If we do not give the primary producer a fair return, we cannot have a healthy economic condition. Roughly speaking, one-half of our population is in agriculture while another substantial portion is engaged in the fishing industry. Then we have our lumbering and mining, both major operations. All of these activities are of immense importance to Canada. If this great body of activity is not assured a reasonable and fair price for its efforts, there cannot be

a healthy economic condition in the state. Let me continue with the reference the report makes to this board, which I submit is quite appropriate at this time. They recommend further:
Through successive steps the board might then proceed to action in connection with disabilities of the industry in something approaching the following order:
(1)	The elimination of misrepresentation of varieties and grades of fish as now prevailing in the retail markets in Canada.
I pause there to interject what I said a moment ago. One of the difficulties in the interior part of Canada, particularly in the densely populated parts of old Ontario, is the lack of accurate information as to the varieties and uses of fish. The minister and his predecessor have done a good deal to improve this condition. Lately we have had a number of broadcasts by some charming lady whose name I have forgotten. All this is useful work, but it merely touches the surface. I continue:
(2)	The establishment of a higher standard of quality of fish marketed in Canada by regulating the conditions under which fish, and especially fresh fish, may be handled.
There is a long story there which might be elaborated.
(3)	The establishment of adequate inspection of grades as affecting products for the Canadian and export markets.
(4)	The elimination of consignment shipments.
This is something which might very well engage the attention of the government.
(5)	The elimination of cut-throat competition and other unsound trade practices.
This could be done by making the trade and industry commission a functioning body. In saying that, I do not intend to reflect upon the late Mr. Justice Sedgewick. During his excellent administration his time was fully occupied with the tariff board; the trade and industry commission was a mere incident. It has never been given the consideration or support which it deserved. Such matters as I have mentioned ought to be referred to the suggested board for its consideration and finding-the elimination' of cut-throat competition and other unsound practices; the direction of surplus production of fish through channels calculated to bring the most profitable financial return. Let me say this in connection with the export business, whether in fish or in any other product. It is possible that with the growing control of markets the world over, the nation as a whole will be forced to take some part in the export of certain of our primary products. I shall not go
further into that at the moment. There is this other question which ought to be referred to the board: a thorough survey of conditions surrounding, as well as the disabilities retarding. development of existing and potential export markets.
These are some of the suggestions that were made. I do not see why such a board as that recommended by the price spreads commission has not been set up before this. Even though there may be a question of jurisdiction, such a board could in my opinion, through the effect of publicity alone, as I have said in this house before in regard to other matters of the kind, where jurisdiction is in question, do a great deal of good.
Let me come back to the immediate issue before us, namely, whether or not within three days to issue licences for these trawlers. I suggest to the minister that for this year we give the fishermen a break. Let us have the corporation do the suffering, if there is to be any suffering, refuse the licences for the trawlers this year, and see what happens. The suggestion is made that if the licences are refused, there will not be a- supply of fish. Very well; let us prove it. Why should we always make the fisherman the goat? Why must we always do nothing for fear of interfering with some large corporation operating trawlers, for fear that they might peradven-ture suffer, on the other hand ignoring the interests and repeated requests of the fishermen? Let us this year reverse the process and refuse the licences for the trawlers. Let us give a test to this request which the fishermen have made, and see if we cannot improve their conditions. At the end of the year, if we see that we have actually improved the conditions of the fishermen, and if there should be some loss or alleged or supposed loss on the part of the corporation, it will be a question of balancing advantages and disadvantages.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this question. I do not know that I would have spoken this afternoon except for the remarks made by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens). He seemed to assume that the issue here was one between the interests of the fisherman and the interests of the big companies or of one big company, and of course after my hon. friend, with his parliamentary experience and forcefulness, repeats that a number of times hon. members and others are perhaps likely to assume that it is the real issue. The question here is not whether parliament or the minister should act in the interests of the Maritime National Fish company or in the interests of the fishermen of Nova Scotia. The question here is what is in the interests of the fishermen of Nova Scotia.
I should like to say a few words about the background of this matter and about the trawler issue generally. I have listened to discussions in this house during many sessions, and the situation does not develop a great deal as the years go by. There are, however, some slight changes.
As has been pointed out, there are fishing on the banks off the shores of Nova Scotia, the 'banks of the north Atlantic, about three hundred American and foreign trawlers. Canada has, all told, three trawlers under licence, all three owned by one company, the Maritime National Fish company, which has its head office at Halifax and does business

there. It used to be said that the Maritime National Fish company was a United States owned corporation, and that fact was always stressed in the debates; but since 1937 that can no longer be said, because the company, a Canadian corporation, is now widely owned in the maritime provinces. The question, however, is this: Shall the Maritime National Fish company be granted a renewal of its trawler licences?
As to the effect of that, if it were done, I want to trace the facts in detail as I see them. Hon. members must realize that in Nova Scotia there are many types of fishing for ground or bottom fish. There is schooner fishing. The centre of the schooner fishing industry is, I suppose, the town of Lunenburg from which the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Kinley) comes. There are the inshore fisheries, which extend almost all around the shores of Nova Scotia. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Pottier) is chiefly interested in the inshore fisheries. East of Halifax, along the long shore-line of eastern Halifax, Guysborough and Richmond, are a large number of inshore fishermen. That is where conditions became desperate a few years ago, and conditions there are still bad. That is the home of the cooperatives. That is where these priests, clergymen and others have taken an interest in the conditions in their various communities and have organized cooperative stores, credit unions and cooperative lobster packing plants, and they have made some progress in improving the economic condition of the people.
In considering the fishing problem of Nova Scotia, I am not ignoring the problem in my own constituency, or the problem in the constituency of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare; and there is some problem, not nearly as serious as in the eastern constituencies, in the constituency of the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg. Ordinarily, however, we think primarily of the problem that exists in the great eastern district, with a large population and a small production, and its poverty. What sort of business does the Maritime National Fish company at Halifax carry on? It carries on predominantly
a fresh unfrozen fish business. Hon. members this afternoon have not made any reference to the distinction between the fresh unfrozen fish business and the fresh frozen fish business. Perhaps the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg did; I do not know; but I do not think a clear distinction was made between the fresh unfrozen fish business and the fresh frozen fish business. There is all the difference in the world between the two, and that difference is at the root of the question. It is that distinction which makes the question a difficult one, not a one-sided question as the hon. member for Kootenay East would have us think.
A distributor who carries on a fresh unfrozen fish business must get the fish into the hands of the consumer a very few days after they leave the water, and that means that if there are periods of a week or two weeks during which, on account of storms or for any other reason, the fish cannot be landed at the port and sent forward, the fresh fish business passes into the hands of somebody else. It passes into the hands of suppliers of competing fresh fish, other food products or other kinds of fish. At any rate, it goes. Hon. gentlemen may say there should not be any fresh unfrozen fish business, and there is something to be said for that position in general. It may be said that it would be desirable if all fresh fish that was marketed could be put on the market as frozen fish. But parliament cannot decide the taste of the consumer. The consumers of Montreal, Toronto and other places to which this cod and haddock go from Nova Scotia ask for fresh unfrozen fish and demand that they get it. What I want is a
fishing industry producing a large volume of fish. I want to see the fishing industry of Nova Scotia producing greater wealth than it is to-day. Admitting that this can be done with fewer men, the fact remains that if there is more wealth produced there will be a greater expansion in business, there will be increased employment and improved conditions for the province. It cannot be possible
that all hope of expanding markets for the province of Nova Scotia has ceased. A few years ago there were markets abroad for a much larger volume of fish. If my memory serves me aright-and I think it does-in 1926 eleven trawlers were operating out of Nova Scotia. Was your fishing industry at that time in the state in which it has been lately? Have you improved conditions as you have gradually moved towards the elimination of the trawler? You have not. Conditions have become worse and worse as time has gone on.
In times of depression you come back to fish, and come back to it steadily. The movement of men into inshore fishing decreases the price received for fish, demoralizes the market and ruins the industry which you seek to create. I ask for fair treatment and fair consideration of those men who are actually seeking to expand the industry in Nova Scotia by using the best means available.
A few moments ago the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) referred to the fact that a fairly large factory had been closed at Canso. Let me ask this question: What would happen in any industry if a factory were being operated which did not pay? When the men who own a factory have to take a loss, what follows? That means a decrease in the capital invested in the industry. What does a decrease in the capital invested in an industry mean? That affects the prosperity of your industry. This industry in Nova Scotia depends upon whether it is able to expand foreign and domestic markets. That cannot be done unless there is capital available. The industry depends upon the cooperation of capital.
There is the memorable remedy which can be applied to this or any other problem. There must be an extension of freedom to men to do what they want to do. I do not want to see them restricted by being forced to have their trawlers built in Canada. Last year I found out something about the cost of building trawlers in Canada, compared with having them built in Great Britain. There are some ardent souls who are so anxious to have trawlers built in Canada that they would be willing to have these companies pay double the price they would have to pay to have them built in Great Britain. It is only by the extension of economy; it is only by lowering your costs, that you can operate successfully in this highly competitive market. Here as everywhere freedom is necessary, and I ask the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud) to consider the extension of freedom to the Canadian fishing industry.

Mr. Speaker, much has been said this afternoon about the steam trawler, and I am sure the discussion we have heard will bring back fond memories to many of the older members. This question has been debated on many occasions, and the same arguments have been advanced from different sides of the house. The last two memorable occasions upon which it was debated were in 1929 and 1930. Before 1929, steam trawlers were permitted to operate off the shores of Canada without too much restriction or regimentation, 'but at that time parliament thought it advisable to regulate trawlers.
For those who are not familiar with fishing terms-and I am sure there are some in this house-may I say that three methods of fishing are used by those who fish on the Atlantic coast for what is known as ground fish, that is cod, haddock and whitefish generally. First, there is the old method of hook and line which has been in use for the last 300 years. Men go off the shore in small boats with a hook and line and try to catch the cod with bait. As soon as they have sufficient fish in their boats, they come to shore to dispose of them as best they can.
Then, there is the more modern method of using the Lunenburg schooner. This type of schooner is called the Lunenburg schooner because the first schooners were built at that port. The fishing is not done from the schooner proper. The schooner is a large boat propelled by a diesel engine. It goes to the grand banks or off the shore and stays several days, generally being manned by a crew of about twenty-five men. Each of these schooners has ten or twelve dories, small wooden boats, which are lowered to the sea when the schooner is out on the high seas, and from which two fishermen fish with hook and line. The success of their catch depends upon the weather and other conditions; when the dory is full, it returns to the schooner, its fish is put into the schooner's stores, and finally the schooner brings its whole catch back to port.
But there is another method which has been described as the trawler method. The trawlers are large boats of the mine sweeper type. As a matter of fact, during the war all our steam trawlers were used as mine sweepers. They are operated by steam, and the fishing is done mechanically. The trawler fishes with a bag which is dragged along the bottom of the sea; when full, the bag is raised with a mechanical derrick and the fish are dumped on to the deck of the trawler. The operation is very similar to the operation of purse seiners

on the west coast. It is obvious to those who have seen either the purse seiners on the west coast or the trawlers on the east, that the trawler method enables the operators to catch a large quantity of fish in a relatively short time, and the fish are not kept lying exposed for a long time to sun and weather. That helps to preserve the quality of the fish when it is offered to the consumer.
Trawling is not a new method of fishing; it has been in operation in the old world for many, many years. It was only in 1908 that a company in Nova Scotia decided to try to develop a fresh fish business in Canada by the trawler method. The records of the department show that before the year 1908 there was hardly any fresh fish, unfrozen, sold in Canada, and the very little quantity that was sold on the Toronto and Montreal markets was imported overnight from Boston, or Portland, Maine, and then distributed and consumed. Thirty years ago most of the fish consumed in Canada was dried, salted, pickled or processed fish. But these people had vision and decided to try to capture whatever market there was in this country for fresh fish, and to expand that market if possible.
The department, working in cooperation with these people, approached the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian National express to secure transportation facilities for the delivery of fresh fish from the Atlantic coast to inland markets. When it is realized that the nearest market of any importance to the Atlantic coast is about fifteen hundred miles from the source of production, one appreciates the difficulties of transporting fresh caught fish and keeping it fresh until it is distributed to the consumers in Toronto and Montreal. But that is something which the trade has been able to accomplish in this country. Canada is now recognized as having the best transportation and distribution facilities of any country in the world for marketing fresh fish far from the source of production. The national railways, in cooperation with the government and the industry, helped to develop markets in the large consuming centres, with the result that from 1925 to 1927 there were about twelve trawlers operating from the coast of Nova Scotia to supply the needs of this expanding market.
After the war, people on the Atlantic coast went into fishing more extensively than before, and a far greater number were engaged in the industry. There was a good market in the United States and the fishing industry on the Atlantic coast expanded. In the winter

Fishing Industry-Beam Trawlers
of 1926-27, the weather was very mild and huge quantities of fish were caught by the inshore fishermen, the schooner fishermen, and the twelve trawlers. There was a glut on the market and prices slumped. The natural result followed, and the claim was made that there was no profit in fishing. The hook and line fishermen blamed the trawlers for the predicament they were in, and so the government of the day appointed a commission of five members, headed by Mr. Justice Maclean, to study the problem. On this trawler question the commission divided, four reporting that the trawlers should be abolished, and Mr. Justice Maclean filing a minority report that the use of the trawlers should be restricted and regulated. The government, as a consequence, decided to regulate the use of trawlers. The then Minister of Fisheries, now Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), went down to the Nova Scotia coast, and upon his report regulations were made whereby the use of trawlers was limited and a tax was imposed on fish caught by trawlers to compensate the inshore fishermen for the loss of revenue in their vocation. Two years afterwards, the courts declared these regulations ultra vires, and the situation reverted to practically what it was before 1929.
Parliament in the session of 1931 went fully into the question again and referred it to the fisheries committee, which investigated and made a report, and on that report are based the regulations which have since governed the licensing of trawlers up to this date. I might as well put on the record the regulations of 1931. Section 56 of the Fisheries Act is the one which applies to trawlers. It reads:
56. (1) Every person shall be guilty of an offence, and shall incur therefor a penalty of not less than one hundred dollars and not more than two thousand dollars, recoverable with costs upon summary conviction, who at any time, except under licence from the minister-
(a)	with intent to fish or to cause any other person to fish with a vessel that uses an "otter" or other trawl of a similar nature . . .
That is a positive enactment in the fisheries act. Subsection 2 reads:
(2) No such vessel shall carry on fishing operations from or to any Canadian port or ports, unless such vessel is registered as a British ship in Canada and is owned by a Canadian or by a body corporate incorporated under the laws of the Dominion of Canada or of one of the provinces thereof, and having its principal place of business in Canada.
I can skip subsection 3, which has no bearing on the discussion. Subsection 4 reads:
(4) The minister may determine the number of such vessels that shall be eligible to be licensed.
Since 1931, the number of vessels has been limited by the minister by virtue of the power conferred upon him by this subsection, and the number has remained the same until the present date. Subsection 5 reads:
(5) Regulations may be made under the provisions of section thirty-four of this act-
(a)	prescribing the form of licence;
(b)	specifying the evidence to be submitted with an application for a licence;
(c)	fixing the conditions under which a licence shall be issued;
(d)	making any other provisions respecting licences.
This is the legislation that authorizes the minister and imposes upon him the obligation of issuing licences when those who apply for them comply with the provisions of the law. Under subsection 4 of section 56 of the Fisheries Act regulations were made from time to time and revised. There were some regulations in 1929. In 1930 and finally in 1931 regulations were formulated providing:
1. A licence for a fishing vessel using an otter or other trawl of a similar nature, other than a small dragger operated by inshore fishermen, will not be granted, except under the following conditions:
(a) That the applicant for such licence shall furnish the Minister of Fisheries with evidence that will satisfy the said minister, that he cannot obtain an adequate supply of suitable fish to enable him properly to conduct and develop his business from the hook and line fishermen, and that if the licence is granted, the extent of his purchase of fresh fish from the said fishermen will not be adversely affected.
These are the main provisions of the regulations that must be complied with by those who are applying for licences. The minister is being placed in the position of an arbiter or a judge in the matter, and if he is satisfied that the evidence which is submitted to him shows that the person applying for the licence is entitled to receive it, he acts accordingly. I have felt, ever since I have been in office that there was no alternative to issuing the licence, and I have done so for the last three years. True, it puts the minister in an awkward position to have this responsibility placed upon him, but each of us must face his responsibilities and discharge them, and I have tried to discharge my duty as best I could in the last three years.

I have been criticized for having delayed until the last moment the giving of my decision. For that reason I have always delayed as long as possible before making a decision in the matter.
I have before me, up to the present, evidence under oath from two companies. One of these is the Maritime National Fish, Limited-that is the new company-which has applied for three licences, that is, the renewal of the three licences which the company has enjoyed for the last seven years. I have also two applications from General Seafoods, Limited, a United States company that has established a base of operations in Halifax and is applying for these licences.
